4. The adverse presumption should have been drawn against the prosecution on account of non-examination of independent witnesses for which no explanation has been offered by the prosecution and instead interested persons have been examined as witnesses to the occurrence and three of them disbelieved the rest also should have been disbelieved. 

 14. Now let us have a look to the nature of the evidence adduced by the prosecution. The evidence of PWs. 1 and 2 in the trial Court did not at all prove the prosecution case. So the prosecution put in u/s 288 Cr. PC some portion of the evidence of PW 1 and the entire evidence of PW 2 in the Committing Court. The law is that the attention of the witnesses is to be drawn to their evidence in the Committing Court which the prosecution wants to put in u/s 288 CrPC. The attention of the witnesses was of course drawn by the prosecution. But the learned Advocate for the appellants has relied on the decisions made in two cases to show that while the Court has discretion to prefer the earlier statement of witness which has been transferred u/s 288 CrPC to his later statement at the trial, this discretion must be exercised with great care, on a careful scrutiny of the two conflicting statements in relation to all other evidence and circumstances appearing from the record and not on mere surmise or conjecture as to possible reasons for the witness having resiled from his earlier statement. The case referred to are the cases of Lal and 2 others vs the Crown reported in 6 DLR (FC) 38 and of the State vs Umed Ali reported in" 15 DLR, (Dacca) 712. It may be pointed out here that PW 1 is the full brother of the deceased. He had no reason to resile from his previous statements made in the Committing Court. P W 2 Ramiz Ali's evidence at the trial Court was entirely against the prosecution case. Still the prosecution did not declare this witness hostile : but it put in his evidence in the Committing Court u/s 288 CrPC. There is reason to hold that the prosecution followed a novel procedure in challenging the varacity of the witnesses deposing at the trial Court. The prosecution however wanted to offer an explanation for these two witnesses resiling from their previous statements. The prosecution case is that appellant Alkas made a document for 5 Kears of land and registered the same in the name of one Moulana Fakhruddin who was none but a benamdar of these two witnesses and for that land they resiled from their earlier stand as witnesses. This suggestion of the prosecution was totally denied. No document was produced by the prosecution to show that, in fact, there was a transaction relating to 5 Kears of land between appellant Alkas and Moulana Fakruddin. The learned Advocate representing the State has argued that nothing is impossible in these days and that it is common knowledge that a brother may be a fatal enemy of another brother. But without anything in support of the prosecution suggestion in that respect we are unable to accept the contention of the learned Advocate for the State. We rather hold that a witness who changes his position and makes diverse statements at different stages should not be relied upon in a serious charge like this. This view was taken in the two decisions referred to above and we respectfully agree with them. It is evident that the witnesses on whose evidence the learned Sessions Judge had based his decision are highly interested being close relations of the deceased. PW. 1 is full brother of the deceased. PW. 6 lives in the same house with PW. 1 and PW. 2 is the brother-in-law of PW. 6 Abdul Hadi. So he is also related to them. PW. 6 is the cousin of PW. 1. There is evidence that there are a large number of houses all around the house of the deceased and at the time of the occurrence about two hundred people assembled in the house. They heard of the occurrence but none of them is a witness to the case. PW. 1 also says that the neighbours are not witnesses in his case. There is no explanation as to why none of them is a witness in this case. It may be argued that the relation witnesses should not be disbelieved if they had seen the occurrence. It is true, but we have noticed the nature and the character of the relation witnesses and also the qualify of their evidence. We do not, therefore, think it at all safe to rely on their evidence. Non-examination of independent witnesses, particularly some of the neighbours, raises a presumption against the prosecution to the effect that had they been examined they would not have supported the prosecution case that the occurrence took place in the manner and at the place as alleged by the prosecution.
